notes: Exhaust will not reduce true damage.
Exhaust applies its slow and damage reduction as separate debuffs, of which only the slow can be affected by tenacity or cleansed.
Cleanse, however, removes both the slow and the damage reduction.
Using Exhaust on a champion when the target is already affected by that spell will reapply the effect, resetting its duration. It will not increase the effect.
The visual indicator of Exhaust will not reset along its duration, ending prematurely and not appearing for further Exhaust reapplications.

If Teleport was already taken, the quest will instead empower the spell to grant a 35% maximum health shield for 10 seconds after the channel ends. The cooldown of Unleashed Teleport is additionally reduced by 30 seconds.
Teleport calculates the travel time for the dash based on the distance between the user's casting position and the target's location at the start of the channel.
Teleport has a base dash speed of 1000.
The dash speed will be increased to account for the fixed travel time.
Unleashed Teleport has a dash speed of 4500.

If Teleport's current cooldown is greater than Unleashed Teleport's maximum cooldown upon transformation, the current cooldown is reduced to its maximum.
Teleport has no cast time.
Teleport goes on cooldown after the dash ends.
Teleport is disabled while grounded, rooted, or unable to cast. It also cannot be used while in Death Realm.
Nearsight will prevent the caster from using Teleport globally.
Teleport's untargetability does not destroy in-flight projectiles.
The champion's model is hidden while they are dashing with Teleport and instead can be visually seen as a trailing orb.
If there is not enough free space upon landing, the user may land in the nearest open space in the direction of travel.

Neither Teleport's channel nor dash will cancel if the target dies during either effects.
The target's location at the start of the channel will be considered for the destination location of Teleport, not the target's location when the channel completes or the dash ends.
Teleporting to a ward or stealthed trap reveals it to enemies.
The target ward or trap is only revealed if it is within an enemy's sight radius and their sight isn't being obstructed.
The user may select their target for Teleport via the minimap.

When attempting to cast Teleport on a target that is at least 3000 units away, the targeting for the spell has a forgiveness radius of 400 units. This is particularly useful when targeting via the minimap.
Teleport's visual effects can be seen even through the fog of war.
While standing at the end of a wall or other standing out part of terrain, using Teleport slightly increases sight radius just around the corners in the fog of war.
Teleport and Unleashed Teleport will play an 'On My Way' ping on the target.
A timer for Teleport's remaining duration is visible at the target location to all players.

rulePages.title: Template:Tip data/Cast-inhibiting crowd control
rulePages.text:
A unit that is affected by cast-inhibiting crowd control is unable to cast abilities, activate items, or use summoner spells. The following crowd control effects disable casting of all spells and abilities as well as interrupt all channels:
* Airborne
* Forced Action (Berserk, Charm, Flee, Taunt)
* Silence (Polymorph)
* Sleep
* Stasis
* Stun (Suspension)
* Suppression
Note that Disrupt is not a status effect and solely interrupts channels, and thus cannot fall under this classification. However, abilities that would be interrupted by forms of cast-inhibiting crowd control are also interruptible by Disrupt.
Root and Ground only disable movement spells and abilities. Stasis and Suppression are the only crowd control effects that disable all summoner spells from use; all other cast-inhibiting crowd control only disable movement summoner spells.

rulePages.title: Template:Tip data/Spell shield
rulePages.text:
A spell shield refers to one of several effects that have the capacity to negate hostile abilities from applying to the recipient. A spell shield may negate many active effects coming from champion abilities, epic monsters, champion summoned units, and items, but almost none from runes and summoner spells with the only exceptions of Arcane Comet, Unleashed Smite, and Primal Smite which will be blocked.
* See the article for more details.

rulePages.title: Stealth
rulePages.text:
Stealth refers to various positive effects that temporarily conceal a unit from enemies' sight regardless of the Fog of War. Stealth is divided into three categories: Camouflage, Invisibility and Stealthed traps. Camouflage conceals units only while no enemy champion is within the detection radius.
Stealth can be interrupted by the user via certain actions, most commonly casting an attack or ability. A stealthed unit can also be directly revealed by enemy effects that grant true sight.
Stealth should not be confused with vanish, an effect that removes a unit's model and does not interact with the mechanics described here.
== General ==
* While a unit is stealthed, enemies cannot select it, thus allowing it to effectively avoid many incoming threats. Most notably, unit-targeted spells (including basic attacks) cannot target enemies that the user does not have sight of.
* This icon indicates that the unit is exposed to enemies when it normally should not be. It does not necessarily mean the unit is being revealed through stealth—sources of revealing via standard sight and true sight use this same icon.
** Standard sight debuffs on a stealted unit will not render them visible, but true sight will.
* Stealthed units are granted ghosting only while enemies do not have sight of them.
* If a unit is hit by a damaging ability (even if the ability deals no damage) while stealthed, their silhouette's position shimmers for 0.6 seconds, which is accompanied by a visual and audio cue.
* Crowd control effects do not break stealth, with the exception of the forced action effects taunt and berserk, which force the unit to attack.
** Uniquely, the stealth from Guerrilla Warfare is broken if he is knocked airborne.
* Curse of the Black Mist will still grant the Wraith Form buff to allies that have stealth of their own. They will however not be seen as a Wraith while outside of her aura while their own stealth is active.
* If a unit has multiple sources of camouflage, they will be visible based on the smallest detection radius among them.
* If a unit has both camouflage and invisibility, invisibility is prioritized. The camouflage's detection radius will be invalid for the duration of the invisibility and apply again when the invisibility ends.
* Champion clones also have a valid line of sight and therefore can see camouflaged units if the conditions are satisfied.
* Sudden Impact interacts with stealth.
== Camouflage ==
Camouflage
Since a direct line of sight is required in addition to standing within the camouflaged unit's detection radius, note that a nearsighted enemy whose sight radius is smaller than the camouflaged unit's detection radius will not be able to detect their stealth.
Camouflage provides indicators that distinguish the state of the stealth effect.
The indicators are only visible to the stealthed unit and their allies; enemy champions do not need to be visible themselves for the indicators to appear.

== Stealth detection ==
There are various ways for a champion to gain the ability to see stealthed units.
=== Revealing effects ===
True Sight is a form of vision that reveals stealthed units. All turrets have true sight over their area, and there are some champion abilities that apply it as well. Mark is the only summoner spell that applies true sight. The Sweeper Drone specifically reveals stealthed wards and traps.
When a stealthed unit that is revealed due to enemies having true sight over the area leaves that area, the stealthing unit does not experience a fade-out time, but is immediately concealed.
The following abilities grant true sight of the target:
=== Presence detection without reveal ===
The obscured vision granted by Oracle Lens Sweeper Drone is the most commonly accessible form of detecting stealthed champions without revealing them and rendering them targetable. The Drone will expose the detected units' silhouette at regular intervals.
Auto-targeted effects that do not require sight to cast will show whether or not they can cast when an enemy is nearby (by lighting up in the HUD) even if the target in range is not visible. Damage over time effects that repeat over short intervals and are not prevented by the target will cause their silhouette to shimmer regularly, thus indicating their position with great precision.
Direction-targeted abilities (skill-shots) can still hit stealthed enemies, but they will not grant sight of them unless the ability has a stealth-revealing effect. The projectile may play visual and audio cues (e.g. Infected Bonesaw splatter / blood eruption upon impact) which indicate if a stealthed unit is hit and may provide enough knowledge of their whereabouts. Particular cases of skill-shots that do not reveal units but play prominent effects are Light Binding cage VFX and Grasping Roots thorn VFX which show on enemy units' location even if the hit units themselves cannot be seen.
The following abilities are some examples of non-direction-targeted effects that can inform allies of an enemy's presence or compromise the enemy's exact position regardless of stealth.
* Via secondary ability effects that trigger from enemy hits:
** Twofold Hex (recast missile originates from target)
** Blooming Burst (blooms again after hitting an enemy champion)
** Starcall (triggers Rejuvenation and grants its effects)
** Noxious Trap (explodes prominently upon the trap being triggered)
** Vision of Empire (recalls Soul Fragments to the user)
** Arcane Storm (continues following enemies if previously ordered to when the enemy was visible)
* Via other visual effects (VFX) on or toward the enemy's position:
** Hookshot (range indicator)
** Spirit of Dread (drain particle)
** Duskbringer (trail is always visible and follows enemies' position)
** Electrical Surge (Active)
** Burrow Tremor Sense, which specifically compromises the position of any moving unit as a key mechanic
** Blood Hunt trail, which specifically compromises the position of any marked unit as a key mechanic
** Tides of Blood
* Via the availability of Auto-targeted effects that do not require sight of the target to cast or trigger:
** Arcane Shift (Hit)
** Bountiful Harvest
** Lunge (Hit)
** Death Lotus
** Mocking Shout
** Soul Shackles
== Breaking stealth ==
Stealth is lost immediately when starting or completing the attack windup of a basic attack or upon casting an ability (including Recall / Empowered Recall), unless otherwise stated. Using consumables or trinkets does not break stealth. Summoner spells and item actives vary.
=== Summoner Spells ===
The following summoner spells will break stealth upon activation:
* Exhaust
* Hexflash
* Ignite
* Mark / Dash
* Smite
The following summoner spells will not break stealth upon activation:
* Barrier
* Clarity
* Cleanse
* Flash
** The visual effects are not hidden.
* Ghost
* Heal
* Teleport
=== Items ===
The following item actives will break stealth upon activation:
The following item actives will not break stealth upon activation:

* Farsight Alteration
* Eye of the Herald
* Oracle Lens
* Warding Totem
* Scarecrow Effigy

rulePages.title: Damage
rulePages.text:
: Not to be confused with attack damage, a champion statistic, nor conflated with health costs, which are not damage.
Damage is the result of a direct combat interaction between two units: a source unit causes a deduction of a target unit's current health via a damaging spell (or accompanying debuff). Damage takes place in engine time ("instantaneously") and the application itself is formally called a damage instance or damage event.
Invulnerability prevents damage, and shields can protect from it. Damage values can also be modified by the source or the target through damage modifiers. They can also be increased by a percentage due to an event called a critical strike.
Enemies are slain upon dealing enough damage to deplete their health. A champion dealing damage against another champion triggers kill attribution (if it does not slay them otherwise) and, if the damage-dealer is within enemy turret attack range, also triggers the turret's aggression until they exit the turret's range.
== Types ==
The following three damage types exist: Physical, Magic, and True. Each damage event can fall under only one of these three categories.
These three types exist to add variability to gameplay beyond simple deduction of health equal to the source's outgoing damage value, by potentially reducing, or mitigating it instead.
* Physical damage is innately mitigated by armor, a statistic that units possess.
* Magic damage is innately mitigated by magic resistance, a statistic that units possess.
* True damage cannot be mitigated by any innate statistic.
Aside from these innate mitigations, various effects can also reduce outgoing damage by a source (e.g. Exhaust), reduce incoming damage from all or some sources (e.g. Meditate), potentially nullify any damage received (e.g. invulnerability) or prevent an effect, which may or may not be accompanied by damage, from being applied altogether (e.g. spell shield). True damage additionally has the property of being largely unaffected by damage reductions, with the exception of Riposte, which invariably reduces all incoming non-execution damage dealt by sources other than turrets by 100%.
Effects that trigger from damage type will always occur, unless prevented from applying altogether, regardless of its classification.
== Additional classification ==
In addition to types, damage instances can have multiple other classifications to determine and manage interactions systemically.
Note that damage instances can equal zero (i.e. a health deduction, of zero). This is most commonly utilized for triggering kill attribution and minion aggression.
=== Tags ===
The tag system is a restrictive classification applicable to the source of the damage instance. It is restrictive because each tag entails a number of default properties the damage instance can have, and spells that interact with other spells can choose to ignore certain tags. Damage instances can have any combination of these tags, though some combinations are atypical or never found in game. Properties are a secondary classification system, explained further below.
* BasicAttack: Represents the base damage of all champion basic attacks (invariably), most empowered attacks (e.g. Power Fist, Crippling Strike), most attack-like abilities/also referred to as attack-spells (e.g. Mystic Shot, Lunge) and all attack modifiers (e.g. Heroic Swing, Royal Maelstrom, Purge, Runaan's Hurricane Wind's Fury bolts).
** All champion basic attacks, which are tagged with this, apply life steal and on-hit effects through the ApplyLifesteal and TriggerOnHitEvents properties, respectively, as a fundamental mechanic. However other damage tags can have these properties, meaning they are not exclusive to this tag.
* ActiveSpell: Represents most active champion and item abilities, i.e., ones that the player has issued an active command, and paid a cost if applicable, to cast.
** This tag allows triggering ability effects (invariably).
* AOE: Represents damage in an area (Area of Effect) or sometimes across multiple units.
** This tag is usually tied to penalties compared to other damage tags, since area effects are considered easier to apply than single-target effects.
* Periodic: Represents effects repeating at a cadence generally shorter than traditional cooldowns and over a period, instead of at once. The repetition can originate from a continually firing spell (e.g. The Culling, Tormented Shadow) or be applied via a debuff (e.g. Malefic Visions, Poison Trail, Liandry's Torment Torment).
** This tag is usually tied to even stricter penalties compared to AOE and additionally has the property of not expunging sleep.
* Proc: Represents all effects applied as secondary on top of other more interactive effects. This is used for any damage that should not trigger a chain of additional attack and spell effects due to other damage tags on a target. On-hit and spell effects themselves are usually tagged proc.
** This tag is self-limiting; it exists so that effects that trigger from other damage tags do not continuously apply and/or repeat.
* Indirect: Represents effects that are to be considered "not actively or directly sourced by the player themselves".
** In addition to not expunging sleep like Periodic, and being self-limiting like Proc, this tag is reserved for use in other systems that require exclusion of all other damage types. It is rare and any further uses as of 2026 are unknown.
* Pet: Represents all damage originating from champion summoned units, also to defer attribution to their summoner.
* Item: Represents damage originating from most non-champion spells. Despite the name, this includes summoner spell damage against champions, in addition to item abilities.
** This tag is generally exclusionary; it exists so that non-champion-sourced damage is identified and grouped separately from other champion-sourced damage, as a lesser category, and so that it does not remain untagged, for consistency. Damage instances which are supposed to remain unaffected by effects that modify champion attacks or ability damage are also tagged as such.
* NonRedirectable: Represents all damage that manipulates the source of the instance. It has no current known applications, except (presumably) Sleepy Trouble Bubble expunging of sleep specifically. It may be vestigial.
* DoesNotAggroJungle: Represents all damage that should not trigger neutral monster aggression, which includes Friend of the Forest and the regular damage of Gustwalker HatchlingMosstomper SeedlingScorchclaw Pup jungle companions.
* OnHit: Represents all on-hit effects (invariably).
** This tag exists for interaction with effects that modify and/or repeat on-hit effect application.
* Augment: Represents damage dealt by augment systems in modes such as Arena and ARAM: Mayhem (invariably).
** This tag exists for interaction with effects that modify and/or repeat augment effect application.
The same origin spell can have any number of damage instances, even occurring simultaneously. It can also apply different damage instances with different tags depending on the target, or even the number of targets hit (the latter includes effects such as Lay Waste).
In addition to all of the above, damage can be made to ignore shields and other forms of health manipulation internally. This is not handled by any known tags or properties. It is however most relevant for damage that does not fall under any tag.
=== Untagged ===
Untagged damaging effects also exist, which can have completely custom properties, though they are rare. On the , these are referred to as default damage (not official terminology). Some examples are listed below.
* All executes (Elder Immolation, Death from Below, Satchel Charge against turrets, etc), which ignore shields.
* The Nexus Obelisk's damage, which ignores shields.
* Crescendum attack secondary damage.
* Fired Up! when applied via self-cast only.
* Umbral Glaive Blackout ward damage.
* A portion of all zero-damage instance spells, such as Tempered Fate, Time Bomb application, Pillar of Ice displacement, and Ignite application (exists separately to its ticks of non-zero damage).
Untagged effects which also bypass death protection are termed raw damage. In the context of champions, this only includes the Nexus Obelisk's damage against them specifically (it uniquely respects death protection against non-champions) and Cell Division damage redirection. It is however common in other systems, such as the pit Rift Herald Eye damage, the summoned Mercenary self-damage when hitting a turret, Mutated Scryer's Bloom ward damage in the Chemtech Rift, and others.
=== Properties ===
Damage properties determine the behavior of the damage instance. As stated above, tags can imply certain properties as implemented, but apart from ActiveSpell's behavior these are technically completely customizable.
* ApplyAttackRatio: (Unknown)
* ApplyCritical: (Unknown)
* ApplyDamageModifier: When disabled, the damage instance will be unaffected by damage modifiers.
* ApplyLifesteal: When enabled, the damage instance applies life steal. Unlike vamp effects, this is not healing through damage dealt. Healing modifiers that affect life steal also affect spells with this tag.
* ApplyOmnivamp: When enabled, the damage instance applies omnivamp.
* ApplyPhysicalVamp: When enabled, the damage instance applies physical vamp. Due to the stat being unused, this property is likewise deprecated.
* ApplySpellvamp: When enabled, the damage instance applies spell vamp. Due to the stat being unused, this property is likewise deprecated.
* EnableCallForHelp: When enabled, the damage instance triggers enemy minion aggression on the user.
* EnableKill: When disabled, the damage instance will never be able to deal lethal damage. Mostly used for systems other than champion and minion combat.
* RespectDodge: When enabled, the damage instance will be prevented via dodge effects (e.g. Jubilant Veil, Counter Strike).
* RespectImmunity: When disabled, the damage instance will ignore all death protection effects and kill the enemy. Spell shield may still prevent the application of the effect, if applicable.
* TriggerDamageEvents: When disabled, the damage instance will ignore effects that trigger from the damage type and will behave as it were not considered one (except for stat tracking).
* TriggerOnHitEvents: When enabled, the damage instance will apply on-hit effects.
=== Unexpected effect tags ===
These effects have certain tags or combine properties of multiple tags in a manner that renders their behavior unexpected or complicated to players. Note that these are not necessarily considered bugs, however.
* Only tagged AOE (W cone)
* Proc damage that is also ActiveSpell (Aftershock)
* Item damage that is also BasicAttack (Heartsteel, Kraken Slayer)
* Proc damage that is also AOE (Infernum cone damage, I, W)
* Proc damage not tagged AOE (Hextech Dragon Soul, Q Fishbones explosion, I, Q area attack, The Relentless Storm chain lightning, Lightning Crash chain lightning, Luden's Echo)
* Non-AOE damage that actually affects multiple enemies passively (Sentry Infernum, W)
* Always AOE damage that actually potentially affects only a single target (Binding Eclipse, Q, R, R, Q against minions, Q, Red Card, E, Titanic Hydra target and cone.)
* DoT effects not tagged Periodic (I, Aspect of the Dragon).
* Repeating effects not tagged Periodic (W, R, E, R, Q, W, Pocket Pistol, Q secondary hits, E, W, E, Q, R, R, Q).
** Similar effects tagged Periodic (Q additional hits, R, Q additional hits, R)
* Pet basic attacks tagged BasicAttack (Annie Tibbers, Ivern Daisy, Malzahar Voidling and Yorick Maiden of the Mist) - can trigger Infernal Dragon Soul and be reduced by Plated Steelcaps, but cannot apply Conqueror
* Pet basic attacks not tagged BasicAttack (Spiderling, Q, W, Mist Walker, I) - cannot trigger Infernal Dragon Soul nor be reduced by Plated Steelcaps, but can apply Conqueror
* Ability-modified attacks that are not tagged BasicAttack (W)
* Attack additional damage that applies lifesteal but is not tagged BasicAttack (I, Q, Q, I)
** Similar effects that apply lifesteal and are tagged BasicAttack (W, Q and R)

=== Critical strike ===
A damage instance can critically strike when it is implemented as such on an active attack or ability. Damage that critically strikes has been modified by a percentage above 100%, thus deals increased damage. Most critical strikes interact exclusively with critical strike chance, critical strike damage, and Randuin's Omen Resilience. The highest critical strike damage instance is also tracked in the post-game statistics.

;Average damage calculations
: Formula Assumes the Following:
* All amounts are in decimal form.
* DamageBase = the damage that can crit
** Set value to 1.00 to get average damage multiplier
* CritChance = critical strike chance
* CritMod = critical strike modifier/multiplier/ratio
** This affects your Damage Increase from your attack critting
Then the average damage per attack when continously attacking can be calculated with the formula:
\begin{align}
AverageDamage(DamageBase)
& = DamageBase + CritChance \times \Bigl(CritMod - 1 \Bigr) \times DamageBase \\
& = DamageBase \times \Bigl({\color{green}1 +} {\color{orange}CritChance} \times {\color{cyan}(CritMod - 1)} \Bigr) \\
& = DamageBase \times \Bigl( ExpectedDamageMultiplier \Bigr)
\end{align}

;Average damage explanation
Intuitively understand that critical strikes can be considered a 'percent chance' to increase damage by 'some percent' (with variance of course)
along with some math to convert it to a multiplier
Crit multiplier explanation
* For a 175% (1.75x) crit multiplier, this 'some percent' damage increase is 75% (Add 0.75x base damage)
* For a 200% (2.00x) crit multiplier, this 'some percent' damage increase is 100% (Add 1.00x base damage)
* For a 230% (2.30x) crit multiplier, this 'some percent' damage increase is 130% (Add 1.30x base damage)
* For a CritMod (?.??x) crit multiplier, this 'some percent' damage increase is (CritMod% - 100%) (Add [CritMod - 1.00]x base damage)
Some abilities or characters have a crit multiplier attached to them also. (e.g Way of the Wanderer) Simply multiply by that number to get the final result.
Crit chance explanation
With a 25% 'percent chance' to increase damage by 'some percent', this is equivalent to (on average, with some variance) increasing your damage dealt by 25% of your 'some percent' damage increase.
* A 25% 'percent chance' to increase damage by 75% is equivalent to increasing your damage by 18.75% (25% of a +75% damage increase is a 1.1875x damage increase)
* A 1% 'percent chance' to increase damage by 75% is equivalent to increasing your damage by 0.75% (1% of a +75% damage increase is a 1.0075x damage increase)
* A 25% 'percent chance' to increase damage by 100% is equivalent to increasing your damage by 25% (25% of a +100% damage increase is a 1.25x increase)
* A 1% 'percent chance' to increase damage by 100% is equivalent to increasing your damage by 1% (1% of a +100% damage increase is a 1.01x increase)

==Subtypes==
===Resistance subtypes===
See also: Armor and Magic Resistance
Resistance subtypes are a secondary typing system that exists to promote champion classes by diversifying the effectiveness of items and champion match-ups. There is a small selection of effects that are triggered by specific subtypes rather than the above archetypes - e.g. Morellonomicon will trigger on anything with the magic damage subtype, including abilities, basic attacks and on-hit effects (i.e. Wit's End will trigger Morellonomicon on a champion with no other source of magic damage). These are the damage types visible to players in-game.

==Calculating Damage==
: Also see: Damage modifier.
The following effects influence damage as non-zero values, in no particular order of calculation. They may originate from the attacker or the target.
* Percentage damage amplification
* Percentage damage reduction
* Flat damage reduction
* Resistances, meaning armor and magic resistance, against physical damage and magic damage, respectively
* Resistances reduction
* Resistances penetration, meaning armor penetration and magic penetration
Resistances effectively reduce the respective damage subtype (physical or magic) by a percentage. However, "percent damage reduction" is a different, independent effect: abilities such as Unbreakable Will and item effects such as Plated Steelcaps Plating may grant it as a beneficial effect while effects such as Exhaust may apply it as a debuff. Percent damage modifiers stack multiplicatively with the damage reduction achieved through resistances.
After the physical and magic damage is affected by the various reductions, it is applied to the target in health amount. This amount received by the target is called post-mitigation damage.
==Capped Damage==
Some abilities, scaling with target's health, have a capped amount of damage they can deal to a target. This is made to avoid dealing massive damage to targets with a lot of health, most often against only minions and/or monsters.
*If the ability deals enough damage (before damage reductions) to reach the cap, the ability's damage is reduced to the cap and damage reductions are then applied. This means that against a target that has negative armor or magic resistance the ability's post-mitigation damage can be higher than the cap.
==Misconceptions==
The resistance types—physical, magic and true—are often regarded by players to be the archetypal damage types, which leads to a lot of misconceptions.
For example, some players believe that magic damage, ability damage and AP are all interchangeable terms, with even prominent streamers referring to abilities as dealing "AP damage" and "AD damage". This is incorrect. It is possible for basic attacks to deal magic damage (e.g. Thresh with a point in Flay); it is possible for abilities to deal physical damage (e.g. Riven); it is possible for AD-scaling abilities to deal magic damage (e.g. Shyvana); and it is possible for non-magic damage to apply spell effects (e.g. Luden's Echo would trigger on Riven if she chose to buy it, although she's discouraged due to her having no AP scalings).
Similarly, many players believe that life steal and spell vamp are specific to physical and magic damage, respectively. Life steal will apply to anything classified as basic damage (including the magic damage from Takedown and Infinite Duress and true damage from Hextech Munitions), and spell vamp will apply to anything classified as ability damage (including the physical damage from Comet Spear and true damage from Reckless Swing).
